stories.title: Nvidia's Board Moves to Oust the Man Who Built It
stories.story:
Jensen Huang co-founded Nvidia in 1993, spent 33 years turning it into a roughly $4 trillion chipmaker, and became the indispensable human face of the global AI boom. This week, that reign appears to be ending — not over a failed product bet or a missed earnings cycle, but over a tangle of personal scandal with national-security dimensions.

The crisis escalated in layers. First came reports of an affair with a woman U.S. intelligence officials believe was operating as a Chinese spy. Then the New York Times reported a second relationship, with an Nvidia employee. Huang admitted to his board that he had been "unfaithful" to his wife. By Wednesday evening, the Wall Street Journal reported that the board — which hired the law firm Wachtell, Lipton to investigate — was preparing to remove him. Reuters independently confirmed it. Nvidia shares fell more than 9% in after-hours trading, a loss approaching $400 billion in market value if sustained.

The structural problem the board now faces is profound. Nvidia operates without a formal board chair and has published no succession plan. CFO Colette Kress is considered a natural interim choice; prediction markets favor Ian Buck, who runs the data center division. But the deeper issue is that Huang's authority was personal and visionary — he decided what Nvidia would build years before the market knew it needed it. That kind of conviction is not easily transferred to an org chart.

The timing compounds the difficulty. Nvidia's quarterly earnings are due November 17, congressional committees have already summoned Huang to a closed-door briefing on November 18, and Anthropic's IPO is simultaneously repricing the entire AI sector. The question is not just who leads Nvidia next — it is whether anyone can hold together the customer relationships, the roadmap bets, and the geopolitical tightrope walk that Huang managed largely alone.
stories.hook: The most dangerous single point of failure in the AI race turned out not to be a chip — it was a founder.
stories.source: Wall Street Journal / CNBC / Fortune, November 11–12, 2026

stories.title: OpenAI Earns $10 Billion and Loses Even More
stories.story:
For the first time, OpenAI booked $10 billion in a single quarter — a 50% jump from the $6.7 billion it recorded three months earlier. The enterprise business doubled, paid subscribers crossed 100 million, and weekly active users reached 1.2 billion. By the conventional grammar of tech milestones, this is a triumph.

The problem is what sits on the other side of the ledger. Over the same three months, the company's adjusted operating loss widened to $10.9 billion — meaning OpenAI lost roughly $1.09 for every dollar it earned. The absolute loss grew even as the margin improved, a paradox that reveals the core bind: revenue is scaling, but so is the cost of the compute, talent, and infrastructure required to generate it.

The disclosure landed at a charged moment. Anthropic is mid-roadshow for an IPO that could value it at $1.4 trillion, and its own quarterly revenue reportedly runs at $17 billion — nearly double OpenAI's — with a comparatively small operating loss. That gap quietly reorders the narrative of who leads the frontier AI race.

What OpenAI's numbers really show is that the AI industry has built an economy in which scale and losses grow in tandem rather than the usual S-curve where scale eventually crushes unit costs. Compute does not get cheaper when you use more of it; it gets scarcer. The question for investors eyeing an OpenAI IPO expected in 2027 is not whether the company can grow revenue, but whether it can find a cost structure that makes growth worth having.
stories.hook: They're the most-used AI company on the planet, and they still lose more than they earn — every quarter.

stories.title: SoftBank's $3.7 Billion Bet on Turbines That Never Turned
stories.story:
The logic was seductive: AI data centers devour electricity, gas turbines take years to manufacture, and whoever reserved them first would hold the keys to the AI buildout. So SoftBank, through a subsidiary called Silver Bands 7, went on a shopping spree that would have made a robber baron blush. By early 2026, it had reserved more than 13 gigawatts of gas turbine capacity — enough to power a small nation, and more than six times the output of Hoover Dam.

The plan made sense on a whiteboard. It made no sense in practice. Even after fully supplying its planned 9.2-gigawatt Ohio mega-plant, SoftBank was sitting on reservations for far more turbines than it had any project to absorb. As subsequent payments came due, the company walked away from the excess — booking a $3.73 billion charge on nonrefundable advance payments and dragging itself to a $7 billion quarterly net loss.

The collateral damage was immediate. Shares of GE Vernova fell nearly 10% on the news, as investors scrambled to reprice what had seemed like an ironclad order backlog. The unsettling inference: if a buyer with $9.5 billion already paid in advance can cancel and eat the loss, no power-equipment order is truly locked. The entire infrastructure trade — turbines, transformers, grid gear — now carries renegotiation risk the market had not priced a week ago.

Sam Altman's private admission, leaked from a Samsung executive briefing, sharpened the point: demand for AI compute has been systematically double-counted, with middlemen and neoclouds inflating their own projections. SoftBank's turbine bill is what happens when exuberance meets an engineering timeline that cannot be rushed.
stories.hook: The AI boom's first real casualty wasn't a startup — it was a $3.7 billion pile of turbines nobody needed.
stories.source: Wall Street Journal / Tom's Hardware / Inside AI, November 11–12, 2026

stories.title: Anthropic's IPO Roadshow Puts a Price on the AI Era
stories.story:
For years, the value of frontier AI was a number whispered between venture capitalists in side rooms. This week it became a public fact. Anthropic, maker of the Claude chatbot, is on its IPO roadshow targeting a fully diluted valuation of roughly $1.4 trillion — pricing 825 million shares at $70 to $78 each and looking to raise up to $64.4 billion in what would rank among the largest public-market debuts in history.

The number is striking not just for its size but for what it concedes. Earlier in the year, analysts and insiders had been bandying about $2 trillion. The climbdown to $1.4 trillion reflects two sober realities landing at once: AI infrastructure costs are staggering — Anthropic carries roughly $900 billion in purchase and lease commitments — and AI stocks have been volatile enough to make institutional buyers hesitant. Some buyers discussed pushing the valuation even lower, toward $1.1 to $1.2 trillion, before the company held the line.

The revenue story, however, is genuinely extraordinary. Anthropic generated $33.2 billion in the first nine months of 2026, compared with just $2.5 billion in the same period a year earlier. Its annualized run rate had hit roughly $81 billion by October 31. The gap between that growth and the discounted IPO price is itself the story: even a company growing at over 1,000 percent annually must negotiate with a market that has grown wary of AI promises.

The private placement running alongside the IPO tells its own tale. AMD, Broadcom, Google, Micron, Microsoft, Nvidia, and TSMC are collectively buying $26 billion in shares at the IPO price — Google and Nvidia taking $10 billion each. The companies supplying Anthropic's chips and cloud capacity are also becoming its shareholders. Shares are set to begin trading on the Nasdaq under the ticker ANT on or around November 19.
stories.hook: When the companies selling you the picks and shovels also buy your stock, the gold rush has entered a new phase.

stories.title: The 10-Year Yield Hits 5% and the Fed Isn't Done
stories.story:
The number that governs American financial life — the yield on the 10-year Treasury note — has climbed back to 5%, and this time the catalyst is a one-two punch that is hard to dismiss. October's core inflation came in at 0.3% month-on-month, a tick above expectations. Then Fed Governor Christopher Waller said, in terms unusually direct for a central banker, that a reading at that level would make a half-point December hike worth serious consideration. Markets did not wait for the December meeting to react.

The 2-year Treasury yield — the instrument most tightly tethered to Fed policy expectations — posted its largest single-day surge since April 2025, jumping 17 basis points to 4.74%. The dollar index pushed toward 103, its strongest since May of last year. Gold fell. The 30-year mortgage rate jumped 12 basis points to 7.30%. These are not independent data points; they are the same story told in four different markets simultaneously.

The mechanism is straightforward but the stakes are not. The 10-year yield is the discount rate that sits beneath every asset valuation, every corporate financing decision, every housing market. When it touches 5% — and especially when it threatens to stay there — it reprices the future. Homebuilder stocks dropped 2.5% on the inflation print alone. CME FedWatch now shows a 100% probability of a December hike, with roughly 11% of bets on a full half-point move.

The deeper implication is structural: the Fed is hiking into an energy shock, with Brent crude near $93 a barrel, while the bond market has already tightened conditions considerably without the central bank's help. The question heading into December is not whether rates rise, but whether the Fed — still not satisfied — decides to accelerate. If Waller's view spreads to colleagues, the cost of capital could reset upward again just as the mortgage market and corporate credit markets were beginning to stabilize.
stories.hook: The bond market just told you the Fed isn't finished — and the mortgage market is the first place that lands.
stories.source: Daily Forex / CNN Markets / USA Herald, November 11–12, 2026
